newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan investors shun call to slow China projects.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan investors shun call to slow China projects.

text.p: Taiwan business leaders on Friday shrugged off potential risks that could surface following the death of China's patriarch Deng Xiaoping, vowing not to halt investments on the rival communist mainland.

Taiwan's Nationalist government openly urged investors to approach China's alluring markets with caution, suggesting that political uncertainty expected to follow Deng's death would increase investment risks.

"Although the mainland's economic opening policies will not go backward, the economics ministry urges Taiwan businessmen to take political risks into consideration when planning medium- to long-term investments," economics minister Wang Chih-kang said.

Under an unofficial thaw begun a decade ago, some 30,000 Taiwan firms have pumped well over US$25 billion into China despite a bitter political rivalry that has divided Taiwan and China since a Chinese civil war ended in 1949.
Economics officials cautioned that the risks of investing in China may increase because Deng's passage opens the door for a rethinking of policies he championed.
Taiwan investors said Deng's death was no cause for alarm.
"We have not thought of quitting our investment projects on the mainland," said Kao Chin-yen, chief executive officer of Taiwan's top China investor, President Enterprises.
"Deng's death was something all businesses were expecting so there is no reason for them to be nervous," said Kao, also chairman of Taiwan's Chinese National Federation of Industries.
President expects to begin reaping new profits in 1998 through a number of investments in China, Kao told reporters.

The food giant alone has poured US$900 million into food processing and other investments on the mainland, although it froze plans for a major power station in Hubei province in 1996 after Taipei called for a slowing of mainland investment. Sampo group chairman Chen Sheng-tien said there would be no change in his group's growing mainland projects.
"Ties across the Taiwan strait should be able to improve and become more peaceful in the future," Chen told reporters.
Sanpo, an electronics manufacturer, has invested over US$60 million to set up five China plants, three of which have entered full production.
Chairman Wang Yung-ching of Taiwan's leading industrial enterprise, petrochemicals giant Formosa Plastics, said he expected no expect drastic changes in China's economy in the post-Deng era.

"The 1.2 billion people on the mainland have begun to taste the sweetness of the economic reforms on the mainland, which have brought improvement in their living," Wang told Taipei's Commercial Times.
"This is an unblockable trend," Wang said.
This confidence in people's economic self-interest was why Formosa found the vast mainland market so promising, he added.
Formosa has tripped on Taipei's 1996 appeal to slow China investment to avoid becoming politically vulnerable through over-exposure in the market of Taiwan's only adversary.
Taipei vetoed Formosa's plan to finance a US$3 billion power complex in coastal Fujian province, though local media have said it would carry out the project through a U.S. affiliate.
The economics ministry's Investment Commission said Taiwan had no plans to ease controls on mainland investment.

"Before relations between the rival sides of the Taiwan strait improve, the government needs to control Taiwan investment projects on the mainland," commission executive secretary Tsai Lien-sheng told Reuters.
Taiwan still bans direct contact with and investment in China, obliging investors to route capital through Hong Kong.
All investments of US$1 million or more require approval of the Taiwan government.
